With the three fields below it, it is the key the scanner groups a large candidate's locations by (`kinds`), written onto the location so that a consumer can re-derive the grouping from the document alone and never has to re-run the patterns to learn why two lines are the same kind. WHERE NO CLAUSE CAN BE NAMED IT CARRIES THE READING INSTEAD, prefixed so the two can never be confused: `raw:clauses_split_raw_vs_comment_blanked[raw 3 / blanked 7]` (one clause fired on the line as written and another on the comment-blanked text), `joined:only_on_the_joined_construct` (the fold, not the line, is what fires), `unattributed:no_clause_fires_on_this_line` (the location's evidence is elsewhere - a value hop, an absorbed enclosing construct, a corroboration in another file). A prefixed value is never a clause number and is not compared with one.

matched_token.description: WHAT THE CLAUSES MATCHED, folded: edges trimmed of punctuation, case folded, `_` and `-` dropped; several spans deduplicated, sorted and joined with `+`. Where no clause could be named it is the whole line folded one level coarser and cut at 120 characters. IT IS THE MATCHED SPAN AS THE CLAUSE MATCHED IT and is never widened to the surrounding token: widening pulls a whole URL, hash and all, into the key and turns one kind into one kind per line, which is the failure the census exists to remove. Present exactly where `clause` is. Such lines still group by rule, clause set and context class, which is what the corpus-wide measurement of 2026-09-17 counted them at; widening the span to make the string non-empty would change the key and part the scanner from its own oracle.

context_class.description: THE SYNTACTIC POSITION the match sits in - one of seventeen, listed here in the order the existence-class reading plan visits them: the code shapes `sql`, `declaration`, `call`, `object-key-or-param`, `member-access`, `identifier-use`, `config-entry` first, then `translation-entry`, `string-literal`, `html-attribute`, `import-specifier`, `prose-doc`, `comment`, `css-declaration`, `manifest-entry`, `lockfile-entry`, `other`. It is what keeps a locale catalogue from crowding the one migration out of the seat's 70 groups, and it is part of the kind key, so a call and a comment carrying the same token are never one kind. THE ENUM IS CLOSED ON PURPOSE: a class the engine invents and nothing reads would silently re-order the reading plan, so a new class is added here and to the plan's order in the same change. Present exactly where `clause` is.

sub_shape.description: THE LINE ITSELF, folded outside the matched spans, as a 16-hex digest - how alike two members of one kind really are. Everything outside the match is normalised (string interiors emptied, digit runs to `0`, case and inner separators folded, whitespace collapsed) and the match is kept byte for byte, so two locations with the same digest are the same line up to that normalisation. It is NOT part of the kind key: it is the second level a seat disposes at when one kind merges constructs that must be seen separately - 3 of one large tree's 20 largest kinds do. Present exactly where `clause` is.

dataflow.description: Optional trace from source to sink, where the engine can produce one.

context_questions.description: Questions that must be answered from the surrounding code before this candidate can be adjudicated. At least one, which is rule.schema.json's own requirement of the rule this is copied from: a detector hit on its own never establishes non-compliance, and an empty list would say the opposite by omission.

unanswered_preconditions.description: The applicability_preconditions of this candidate's rule that name a ScanProfile field the profile does not answer, verbatim. Present only when non-empty. THIS CANDIDATE WAS RAISED ON AN OPEN PREMISE AND THE READER MUST BE TOLD SO. Before 2026-08-25 an unanswered precondition removed the rule from the scan, so no such candidate existed; the rule now runs and its candidates reach layer 2 carrying the open question. It is a question to put to the person running the scan, never a fact to infer from the code, and it is not a reason to drop, downgrade or defer the candidate.

declared_inapplicable_preconditions.description: The applicability_preconditions of this candidate's rule that the profile ANSWERED in a way that puts the rule out of scope, verbatim. Present only when non-empty. THE PERSON DECLARED THIS RULE'S SUBJECT OUT OF SCOPE, AND LINES IN THIS TREE MATCHED THE RULE'S PATTERNS ANYWAY. Read it as a disagreement to put back to them, and the scanner may resolve it in neither direction, because a fact about the product is asked of the person and never inferred from source vocabulary. NOT "the detector found the construct", which is what this said until 2026-08-27, and NOT a two-way choice between a wrong answer and a wrong candidate: whether a matched line is on the rule's subject is the question layer 2 exists to answer, and this candidate's own evidence_template is frequently explicit that the match does not establish it; and the project's own harvest classes 8 of its 21 recorded cases as ones where the declared answer is right AND the candidate is legitimate - an answer about the shipped product beside a line in tooling, a test fixture or a dependency, or a rule whose construct is wider than the question the person answered. It is not a reason to drop, downgrade or defer the candidate. Until 2026-08-27 the answer removed the rule from the scan before it read a line, so no such candidate could exist and the document reported state: not-evaluated; measured over the eight pass-1 runs of 2026-08-26 that accounted for 21 of the 69 located misses, the largest class after vocabulary. A SIBLING OF unanswered_preconditions AND NEVER THE SAME FIELD: that one says nobody answered, this one says somebody answered no and the scanner found something anyway. A candidate can carry both.

legal_basis_refs.description: Citations backing the rule, so a reviewer can go to the source instead of trusting the tool.

reading_class.$comment: THE SINGLE ORIGINAL OF THIS SHAPE IS rule.schema.json's 'reading_class', where the field is declared with the full prose of what each value means; this is the same shape restated for the candidate the scanner copies it onto, because a candidate item is additionalProperties:false and would otherwise refuse the field outright. THE SHIPPED CLI IS NOT ONE OF THEM and an earlier wording of this comment named it in error: the CLI never compiles this document at all, and product/packages/cli/src/schema-validate.ts is in any case the one loader that ALREADY resolves cross-file references, through its 'register' option, which verdict-verify.ts uses today to compile verdict.schema.json beside declarations.schema.json. Making it resolve means changing all eight tool-side loaders of the document contract, which is a wider decision than a merge.
reading_class.description: The rule's own reading class, copied verbatim onto every candidate that rule raises (scan.ts). It says what ONE answer of this rule covers and therefore how much of a candidate one adjudication seat reads before it may rule; it changes nothing about what the patterns match or which locations are written. ABSENT MEANS 'per-location', which is how every rule was read before this field existed. The single original is rule.schema.json, which carries the full description of each value.

class.description: One question for the installation, a list, one question per matched line, or a rule whose questions are of more than one shape. See rule.schema.json for what each obliges the seat to read.

item.description: What one entry of the list is, in the rule's own words. Prose for a human and never matched against anything.

elements.description: The parts of the duty the rule's own question text walks, one entry each, copied verbatim from the rule (design section 2 evidence rule E3). The single original is rule.schema.json's 'reading_class.elements', which carries the full description of what may be declared here and what may not. A seat's evidence is checked element by element against this list: per element either an evidence entry with role 'element' and this name, or a recorded search whose 'for' is this name.

name.description: A short identifier for the element, matched exactly against an evidence entry's 'name' and a recorded search's 'for'.

question.description: The 1-based position of the question whose text walks this element.

text.description: The element in the rule's own words, so a reader of a verdict can see what was asked without opening the rule.

item_source.description: Where an item's identity lives, which decides whether any machine can check the list is complete. 'token' is the case the coverage gate claims completeness on; 'reading' is the case no gate can claim at all.

limbs.description: For a 'mixed' rule, the questions that depart from the rule's own class, mapped onto context_questions BY POSITION.

question.description: The 1-based position of the question in the rule's own context_questions array.

class.description: How this one question is answered. 'mixed' is not available here - a limb that is itself mixed is two limbs.

item.description: As 'item' above, for this limb's list.

item_source.description: As 'item_source' above, for this limb's list.

finding_role.description: The rule's role, copied verbatim from the rule's `finding_role` (rule.schema.json, where the values are defined) where the rule declares one, and absent otherwise; absent means `duty_check`. It reaches the adjudicator in the payload's `rules` block, where rule 6c reads it. It changes nothing that fires and no finding id.

duty_about.description: What the rule's duty is about, copied verbatim from the rule's `duty_about` (rule.schema.json, where the values are defined) where the rule declares one, and absent otherwise; absent declares nothing, and only `product_runtime` lets a finding take the not-shipped row.

effective_date.description: Date the obligation behind this candidate starts to apply, copied verbatim from the rule's 'effective_date' (rule.schema.json). It says when the duty starts and nothing else: a rule whose date is in the future still fires and still words its findings as preparation, and no consumer may read this field as a reason to drop, downgrade or defer a candidate. Present only where the rule declares one - the seven baseline-* rules rest on instruments that are all already in force and declare none, and an absent field means 'the rule states no date', never 'the duty applies now'. Wired on 2026-08-13; before that the field was parsed and validated and reached no output at all, which is why eu-cra-001 and eu-cra-002 carry their date inside their title prose.

data_categories.description: The kinds of personal data the rule's author says the matched construct involves, copied from the rule's 'data_categories' (rule.schema.json). It says what kind of data the RULE is about and nothing else: it is not a filter, and it is not a finding about the scanned repository - nothing here asserts that the code actually holds any of the named categories. THESE ARE THE RULE AUTHOR'S OWN LABELS AND NOT A VALIDATED TAXONOMY. rule.schema.json calls them fideslang keys and this schema constrains their shape - lowercase dotted segments, no duplicates - but neither schema constrains their membership: there is no enum, no registry, and the rule base records several keys as unverified house extensions. A census on 2026-08-13 found 33 distinct values over 99 entries carrying three unreconciled splits; the three were reconciled the same day against published fideslang, leaving 30 distinct values over 99 entries with 90 of them fideslang 2.0.0 keys. Parent keys used beside their own children remain (user.device beside user.device.cookie_id) and are legitimate granularity that fideslang itself declares, not a split. A consumer may group or display these strings; it must never read a difference in spelling as a difference in meaning, nor treat the list as exhaustive. Three states, three statements: a populated list names categories, '[]' says the author considered the question and named none (8 rules), and an absent field says the rule states nothing at all (eu-cra-001, eu-cra-002, eu-data-act-001). Wired on 2026-08-13; before that the field was parsed and validated and reached no output at all.

evidence_template.description: The rule author's account of what a match establishes and what it does not — in several rules the only place a limit of that detector is disclosed. Copied verbatim from the rule's 'evidence_template' (rule.schema.json) and passed to whoever adjudicates the candidate. It carries no more authority than 'title': both are the same author's prose about the same detector, and product/plugin/agents/legal-adjudicator.md says what an adjudicator does when they disagree. Not an excerpt of the source and not rendered by any template engine: '{file}' and '{line}' stand for the first entry of 'locations' and are deliberately left unsubstituted, because substituting the first location would misdescribe a candidate that carries several, and because a path out of the scanned repository does not belong inside a field an agent reads as the rule's own words.

remediation_template.description: Suggested change to close the gap. Engineering guidance, not legal advice.

suppressed_by.description: Why the candidate was suppressed (a guard, a precondition, an inline suppression). Suppressed candidates are normally left out of the output entirely; this field is for diagnostic runs that keep them.

depends_on_applicability.description: Applicability verdicts this candidate's own citations turn on. Annotation only: a verdict never removes, suppresses or downgrades a candidate. Attached per citation rather than per candidate because the baseline rules are deliberately dual-cited to CRA and to GDPR Art 32, and the coverage map's instruction is that 'the CRA scope gate never silences the GDPR basis'.

group_part.description: Present only on a candidate that is one PART of a group the engine split because it carried more locations than one agent can be expected to read - the bound is `MAX_LOCATIONS_PER_CANDIDATE` in product/packages/cli/src/scan.ts, 70, which is the measured p95 of the real per-candidate distribution. Absent means this candidate is a whole group, which is the ordinary case. GROUPING IS DECIDED BY EACH RULE'S `fingerprint_spec` AND HAS NO OPINION ABOUT SIZE: a rule declaring `project` emits one candidate per repository however many lines it matched, and until the bound existed nothing in this schema or in the code stopped that from reaching a size nobody reads. It reached it - `recipients-006` on one tree raised ONE candidate carrying 253 locations across 91 files, and that adjudicator recorded in its own words that it sampled representatively rather than confirming each location individually. THE PARTS ARE ONE QUESTION AND NOT SEVERAL FINDINGS: they share a rule, a title, a citation set and a `group_id`, and between them they carry exactly the locations the single candidate carried, in path-then-line order, with none dropped, added or repeated. A consumer counting findings counts groups; a consumer reading locations reads every part. NOTHING HERE CHANGES WHAT FIRES: the same match lines produce the same locations, redistributed. ABSENT BY DEFAULT FROM THE DATE THE KIND CENSUS SHIPPED, AND PRESENT ONLY WITH `--kind-census off`: a candidate above the bound is no longer cut into parts at all but written whole with `kinds` and `reading_plan`, because the question was never several questions and dividing it made every part's seat answer a share of one question. The two are never on one candidate, so a consumer tells the two documents apart by the fields and not by a flag it was not passed.

part.description: 1-indexed position of this part in its group, as `locations[].start_line` is 1-indexed.

of.description: How many parts the group was emitted as. Never 1: a group at or under the bound is emitted whole and carries no `group_part` at all, so `of: 1` would describe a candidate this field is absent from.

group_id.description: `finding_id` of the group as a whole - the fingerprint the single oversized candidate carried before it was split, and the key that ties the parts together. Same shape as `finding_id` because it is one, but NO candidate in this document carries it as its own `finding_id`: every part's id is derived from this value and its part number, so a suppression or a stored verdict keyed on the group matches no part and the group comes back to be looked at, rather than silencing the first 70 locations while the rest surface as if they were something new.

locations_in_group.description: Locations in the whole group, across every part. This part carries a slice of them, so this number is what says how big the question actually is; `locations.length` on any one part does not.

adjudication_group.description: WHICH ADJUDICATION PAYLOAD THIS CANDIDATE BELONGS TO. Present on EVERY candidate, including every candidate of a document in which nothing had to be divided. product/plugin/skills/legal-scan/SKILL.md step 4 hands ONE GROUP of candidates to ONE fresh adjudicating agent, so the group and not the candidate is the thing that agent must read in full - and a per-candidate ceiling on its own leaves the failure it was built to prevent fully reachable. So the scanner computes the grouping itself and bounds it, and NO `key` IN THIS DOCUMENT CARRIES MORE THAN `MAX_LOCATIONS_PER_ADJUDICATION` READING UNITS (product/packages/cli/src/scan.ts, 70) whatever any rule's `fingerprint_spec` does - LOCATIONS where the candidate carries no `kinds` census, which is every candidate of a `--kind-census off` document and every candidate under the bound, and KINDS where it carries one (`reading_units`). A candidate above the bound in kinds is its own key, with `readers` beside it saying how many seats read it before the one that returns the verdict. The bound moved from locations to reading units on the date the kind census shipped, because a project candidate keeps tens of thousands of locations under one key and is read by its kinds. THE KEY IS COMPUTED AND NOT CHOSEN HERE. Without packing, a candidate belongs to the group of its FIRST location's file, and two consequences of that key are stated rather than left to be found - a group can be large because of locations that are not in its own file at all, and the parts of one split group land in different groups whenever they begin in different files. DO NOT CONFUSE THIS WITH `group_part`: `group_part` divides one candidate that carried too many locations, this divides one file's group of candidates that carried too many between them. A candidate can carry both, and counting either as a finding double-counts. AN ORCHESTRATOR GROUPS ON `key` AND NOTHING ELSE: a second grouping rule kept anywhere outside this field is a second copy of a decision two places must agree on. WHERE THE SCAN PACKED ITS PAYLOADS - the default; `--pack-groups off` or PRODUCT_CLI_PACK_GROUPS=0 turns it off - THE KEY IS A BIN AND NOT A FILE: whole candidates are merged, rule by rule, into bins bounded by the same location bound and by at most 3 rules (product/packages/cli/src/scan.ts, MAX_RULES_PER_ADJUDICATION_BIN), because a layer-2 child costs about the same whatever it is handed and the run's bill is therefore the number of children: in one real run more than half the children held ONE location each and cost what a child holding fifty cost. A packed document carries `bin`, `rules_in_bin`, `candidates_in_bin` and `locations_in_bin` on every candidate and an unpacked one carries none of them, so the two are told apart by the fields and not by parsing the key. The four file-group fields are NOT rewritten by the packing and go on saying what they said. The bound holds either way: no `key` in either document carries more than MAX_LOCATIONS_PER_ADJUDICATION reading units, and `reading_units_in_bin` and `reading_units_in_batch` are written wherever those units are not locations.

key.description: The payload. Every candidate carrying this string goes to one agent, and only to that one. UNPACKED (`--pack-groups off`): the file path where the file's group needed a single batch, so an ordinary document reads exactly as it did before this field existed, and `<file>#batch-<n>` where it did not; `file` and `batch` are then the authoritative pair. PACKED (the default): `bin:<n>#<rule ids joined by +>`, where <n> is 1-indexed in packing order and the rule ids are every rule in the bin, sorted - self-describing on purpose, so that a reader of a document, a run log or an audit record can see that a payload is a packed bin and which rules are in it without joining back to the candidates. Every key in a packed document is a bin key, so the two forms never mix inside one document. Either way this is the single string an orchestrator can group on without composing one. IT IS NOT AN IDENTITY ACROSS RUNS, and nothing downstream may treat it as one: bin numbers are assigned per document in packing order, so adding, removing or resizing one candidate renumbers every bin after it and the same question can carry a different key in the next scan (a file key moves too, whenever the candidate's first location moves to another file). A stored verdict, a suppression, a carried-forward premise or any record meant to survive a re-scan is keyed on `finding_id`, which is derived from the scan's own content; this string says only which candidates went to one agent in THIS document.

file.description: The file the group is named for - the file of this candidate's FIRST location. Not necessarily the file every location of this candidate is in: a `project`-scoped candidate brings all of its locations into the group of its first one.

batch.description: 1-indexed batch of this file's group, as `locations[].start_line` is 1-indexed.

batches.description: How many batches the file's group was divided into. 1 means it was not divided, which is the ordinary case - unlike `group_part.of`, which is never 1 because an undivided candidate carries no `group_part` at all. This field is present either way, because an orchestrator must be able to group EVERY candidate without a fallback rule of its own.

locations_in_batch.description: Locations in THIS batch of this file's group, summed across every candidate in it. Never above the bound. It is what one agent is being asked to read only where `bin` is ABSENT: in a packed document the payload is the bin, `locations_in_bin` is that number, and this field goes on describing the file group the candidate belongs to.

reading_units_in_batch.description: READING UNITS in this batch - what the bound is actually in once a candidate may be read by same-kind line groups. A unit is a KIND where the candidate carries a `kinds` census and a LOCATION where it does not, so this equals locations_in_batch for every candidate read line by line. WRITTEN ONLY WHERE A CANDIDATE OF THIS BATCH CARRIES A CENSUS, which is what keeps a `--kind-census off` document byte-for-byte the one this scanner wrote before the census existed. Never above the bound; locations_in_batch beside it may be, by the members the units stand for.
reading_units_in_batch.$comment: Added by unit U2 of the layer-2 unit-of-judgment design. It is the number a reader checks the bound against; locations_in_batch is how many matched lines those units cover.

locations_in_file_group.description: Locations across every batch of this file's group. This is what says how big the file's whole group is; `locations_in_batch` says how much of it this agent holds.

bin.description: 1-indexed bin this candidate was PACKED into, in packing order - a position in this document and never an identity across runs, for the reason `key` gives. Present on every candidate of a packed document and on none of an unpacked one, so its presence is what says which kind of document this is. The bin is the payload: `key` names it, `rules_in_bin` says which rules share it, `locations_in_bin` says how much of the tree it covers, and the file-group fields beside it are no longer the payload.

rules_in_bin.description: The rule ids sharing this bin, sorted, at most MAX_RULES_PER_ADJUDICATION_BIN of them (3). A bin carries one copy of each of these rules' prose to the agent that reads it, which is the cost the location bound cannot see and the reason the rule count is bounded at all. A reader of one candidate can see from this which other rules the same agent was asked about.

candidates_in_bin.description: How many candidates are in this bin - how many separate questions the agent handed it must return a verdict for. A child that returns fewer verdicts than this answered less than it was asked.

locations_in_bin.description: Locations in this bin, summed across every candidate in it. NEVER ABOVE THE BOUND IN READING UNITS (MAX_LOCATIONS_PER_ADJUDICATION, 70): a bin holding a candidate with a `kinds` census counts that candidate's KINDS, so this field - which counts matched lines - may exceed 70 by the members those kinds stand for, and reading_units_in_bin beside it is the number the bound is in. In a document with no census the two are equal and this is what one agent is being asked to read, exactly as it was. The worked case: a candidate of 54,770 locations in 37 kinds is 37 reading units, the seat reads 37 representatives, and this field says 54,770.

seat_model.description: The one model every seat of this bin reads on: the member rules' own `seat_model` (`sonnet` where a rule names none). THE PACKER NEVER MIXES TWO MODELS IN ONE BIN. The person's run-wide `--seat-model` overrides it at launch, and the launch list names every rule then read on a model other than its own setting, with its place count.

reading_units_in_bin.description: READING UNITS in this bin - kinds for a candidate carrying a `kinds` census, locations for one that does not - and what one agent is being asked to read. Never above the bound. WRITTEN ONLY WHERE A CANDIDATE OF THIS BIN CARRIES A CENSUS, so a `--kind-census off` document carries none of these and is byte-for-byte the document written before the census existed.
reading_units_in_bin.$comment: Added by unit U2 of the layer-2 unit-of-judgment design.

reading_units.description: HOW MANY READING UNITS THIS CANDIDATE IS - the unit the bound is counted in from the date the kind census shipped. Its groups where it has a census and its locations where it has none; the reading class decides which (`reading_plan.unit`). Present on every candidate of a document written with the census on and on none of a document written with it off. A candidate of 54,770 locations in 37 groups is 37 reading units and packs like any other; a candidate of 202 groups is its own payload with readers beside it. IT IS NOT A LOCATION COUNT and a consumer sizing a payload's excerpts must use it and not `locations_in_bin`.

readers.description: How many READER children this candidate takes, beside its one verdict seat. Present only where there are any. Readers hold consecutive slices of `reading_plan.order` and return dispositions per kind, never a verdict word; the one verdict seat is unchanged.

payload_bytes.description: THE SIZE OF THIS CANDIDATE'S OWN PAYLOAD FILE IN BYTES, written only where that file is over context_payloads.max_bytes_per_payload and holds this candidate alone. The cap divides a payload of several candidates until every part is under it; a candidate whose payload alone is over it is never divided and never shortened, because a candidate is one seat. This field and oversized are what the run states instead - the exact size the orchestrator is about to paste into one child. It is absent from the payload file itself: the marker travels inside that file, so writing the size into it would change the size.
payload_bytes.$comment: Added by unit S1-a of the layer-2 unit-of-judgment design.

oversized.description: True exactly where payload_bytes is written: this candidate's own payload file is over the cap. A reader of the document tests this field rather than comparing two numbers.

kinds.description: THE CATALOGUE OF SAME-KIND LINE GROUPS of a candidate that carries more locations than one seat reads. Present exactly on the candidates that used to be cut into parts of `MAX_LOCATIONS_PER_CANDIDATE`, and NEVER beside `group_part`: with the kind census on (`--kind-census on`, the default) such a candidate is written WHOLE with this catalogue, and with it off the candidate is cut into parts and carries no census, which is the document this scanner wrote before the census existed. IT IS ONE QUESTION WITH ONE `finding_id`, ONE VERDICT AND ONE REFUTATION: the census says how the question's lines fall into kinds, and `reading_plan` beside it says what a seat reads of them. THE CENSUS NARROWS NOTHING - `locations[]` is untouched and carries every location it carried, and every location is a member of exactly one group. What it removes is one reader opening 58,712 lines one at a time, not any line's presence in the document.

spec.description: The shape of this object. `kind-census-1` is the first; a consumer tests this string and not the scanner's version.

level.description: The clustering level the key is taken at. `L2` is rule + fired clause set + folded token + context class - the level of the corpus-wide measurement of 2026-09-17, whose recorded cells are the gate's oracle for this field's own grouping.

bound.description: The location count above which a candidate gets a census at all - `MAX_LOCATIONS_PER_CANDIDATE` in product/packages/cli/src/scan.ts. Stated so that a document says what its own threshold was.

kinds_total.description: How many groups there are to read - `groups.length`, the `own_evidence` singletons included. This, not `kinds_at_key`, is what the reading plan counts in.

kinds_at_key.description: How many DISTINCT KEYS the locations fall into. It is the number the corpus-wide measurement of 2026-09-17 counted at this key, and it is written beside `kinds_total` rather than instead of it so that the measured number and the reading number are two statements and nobody has to subtract to get either. It is never above `kinds_total`: the own-evidence rule only ever splits a group.

locations_total.description: This candidate's own location count - the sum of every group's `member_count`, and equal to `locations.length`.

sub_shapes_listed_per_kind.description: The cut on each group's `sub_shapes`, stated rather than silent.

groups.description: The groups, ordered by `(rule_id, key)` and then by first member, so two scans of the same tree write them in the same order. Members inside a group are in path-then-line order.

items.description: ONE SAME-KIND LINE GROUP - what one seat reads one representative of.

key.description: The rule id, the fired clause set, the folded token and the context class, joined by a NUL byte. IT IS NOT UNIQUE IN `groups[]` AND NOTHING MAY KEY ON IT: a location whose evidence is not the line it names is its own group (`own_evidence`), so one key can carry an ordinary group beside several single-member ones - on one measured repository, `eu-dsr-001`'s 121 groups fall into 109 distinct keys, all 12 repeats being own-evidence singletons. A GROUP IS IDENTIFIED BY ITS INDEX IN `groups[]`, which is what `reading_plan.order` and `reading_plan.reader_slices` name it by.

own_evidence.description: This group holds exactly one location, because that location's evidence is not its own line - a value hop, a fold, an absorbed enclosing construct, a multi-line span, or a corroboration from another file. Absent on every ordinary group. What makes such a location a candidate is not on any representative's line, so no representative can be read for it, and merging it into a group would hand a seat a line that does not show what it is being asked about.

clause.description: The `clause` of every member - they are equal by construction, because the clause set is part of the key.

matched_token.description: The `matched_token` of every member - equal by construction. Equal by construction, the empty string included (see `candidates[].locations[].matched_token`).

context_class.description: The `context_class` of every member - equal by construction. The reading plan's order is taken on this field.

member_count.description: How many locations this group holds - `members.length`, asserted against it by a workspace test rather than trusted.

members.description: The members' indices into this candidate's own `locations[]`, ascending. THE CANDIDATE'S LOCATIONS ARE IN PATH-THEN-LINE ORDER wherever a census exists - the order the split used before the census replaced it - so an index is a stable name for a location within this document and `members[0]` is the first member in that order. The locations themselves are not copied here: a candidate carrying 58,712 of them would otherwise carry them twice.

representative.description: The member a seat opens: the FIRST in path-then-line order. Never "the most typical", which is a judgement and has no place in a scanner's output.

file.description: The representative's file, copied from the location so that a reader of the census needs no second lookup. Same pattern, and for the same reason, as `candidates[].locations[].file`.

start_line.description: The representative's `start_line`, 1-indexed as every location's is.

files.description: Distinct files the members sit in. One kind spread over 300 files and one kind inside a single generated file are different questions, and this is the field that says which this is.

directories.description: Distinct first-three-segment directories the members sit in - the spread a seat is told about without being handed every member.

sub_shape_count.description: How many distinct `sub_shape`s the members fall into - THE TRUE TOTAL, listed or not, so a consumer can see that `sub_shapes` was cut without counting it.

sub_shapes.description: The largest sub-shapes of this group, descending, with how many members each holds and the index of its first member. Cut at `sub_shapes_listed_per_kind`, which the census states rather than leaving to be inferred; the ones not listed are the smallest. Listing every sub-shape would put one row per location back into the document, which is the cost the census exists to remove.

members.description: How many of this group's members have that digest.

first.description: The index into this candidate's `locations[]` of the first member that has it - the line a seat opens when it disposes at the sub-shape level.

reading_plan.description: WHAT ONE SEAT READS of this candidate, in which order, and what is declared not read. Present exactly where `kinds` is. The plan is a pure function of this document: a consumer can count the agents a run will spend before dispatching any of them, and can say, per large candidate, how many groups the seat will not open. IT DECIDES NOTHING ABOUT LEGALITY - it is a reading order and a bound, and the classes it orders by come from the rule (`reading_class`), not from the scanner's opinion of the code.

spec.description: The shape of this object. `reading-plan-1` is the first (units of kinds or locations, an existence-class tail declared not read, the slack rule); it keeps parsing for old documents. `reading-plan-2` is the full-read form's PLACE PLAN: every matched location is a place, every place is read, `unit` is `place`, `cap` is the seat's place bound (105), `reader_slices` are the consecutive place seats of a candidate larger than one seat, and there is no `not_read` and no `slack_rule`.

reading_class.description: How this rule's findings are read: one question for the installation (`existence`), a list to be enumerated to the end (`enumeration`), one possible violation per line (`per-location`), or a mixture of those limbs (`mixed`).

class_source.description: Where the class came from: `rule` (the compiled rule declares `reading_class`) or `default-per-location` (it declares none, so the candidate is read line by line - which can only read more than a class would, never less). The scanner's embedded copy of annex 4.2 was deleted when the 55 project rules gained the field, and its `design-table-4.2` value went with it. The second value is not dead - `rule.schema.json` leaves `reading_class` optional - and it is what keeps a `per-location` plan from being ambiguous between a declared class and a defaulted one.

unit.description: `place` in a `reading-plan-2` plan: every matched location of the candidate, each read by a seat. In a `reading-plan-1` plan, `kind` for the existence, enumeration and mixed classes; `location` for the per-location one. It is the unit `adjudication_group.reading_units` counts in and the unit `order` indexes.

cap.description: What ONE seat reads - `MAX_LOCATIONS_PER_ADJUDICATION` (70). IT BOUNDS READING AND NOTHING ELSE: scan.ts's own comment on that constant stands - it is a percentile of a cost distribution and not a measured reading capacity.

order.description: The reading order: indices into `kinds.groups`, or into `locations[]` where the unit is the location. A TOTAL ordering of every unit - what no seat reaches is declared not read in `not_read`, never omitted from the plan, so the plan and the census can be checked against each other. For the existence class the order is by context class (code shapes first, prose and catalogues last) and then by member count descending, so that the seat's 70 are the ones a question about the installation is answered from and a locale catalogue never crowds out the one migration.

read_by_seat.description: The verdict seat's own slice, `order[0 .. read_by_seat - 1]`. `0` where readers read every unit.

reader_slices.description: One entry per reader child, each a consecutive slice of `order`, both ends inclusive. Empty where the candidate takes no reader.

from.description: First position in `order` this reader holds, inclusive.

to.description: Last position in `order` this reader holds, inclusive.

oversized.description: A place seat (reading-plan-2) holding ONE place whose payload alone is over context_payloads.max_bytes_per_payload: the place is never cut, it has a seat of its own, and the plan records it (full-read design 1.2, review R15; build unit F2). Absent on every other slice.

summary.description: A summary seat (reading-plan-2; full-read design section 2, build unit F6): the slice holds exactly the places one data summary covers, and its payload holds that summary (`candidates[].summaries[].id` equal to this value) and no row or window for them. Absent on every other slice.

own_name.description: An own-name seat: the person declared the code to be this vendor entry's software (or a fork of it), and every place of the slice names only that entry on a line naming no host or URL under its name. The seat reads every one of them, told the answer and asked one question (the payload's `own_name.question`) in place of the rule's context questions. Absent on every other slice.

slack_rule.description: The slack rule applied: an existence-class candidate of at most twice the cap gets ONE reader for the remainder, so that nothing is left unread for the sake of a few groups.

not_read.description: The units no seat opens, with the reason - the existence-class tail, and nothing else. ABSENT WHERE EVERY UNIT IS READ, which is the ordinary case and every case the corpus has produced so far; it is written only when there is a tail, so that the object's own constraints are probed the day one exists rather than sitting beside a `null` that no value can violate. THE CAP BINDS IN ONE DIRECTION ONLY: while this is present the verdict may be `violation_candidate` or `needs_human` naming the number not read, and NEVER `not_applicable` - a dismissal is a claim about every kind, and 70 of 16,926 cannot carry it.

from.description: First position in `order` that no seat opens, inclusive.

to.description: Last position in `order` that no seat opens, inclusive.

units.description: How many units that is - `to - from + 1`.

reason.description: The verdict rests on the premise established from the groups that WERE read, on the recorded repository-wide search for the duty's elements, and on this catalogue. It is the only reason the scanner writes; the others in verdict.schema.json's enum are a seat's to write.

rules_without_candidates.description: Every rule the loaded bundle shipped that raised NO candidate on this tree, with what it was looking for. THE ABSENCE OF A FINDING IS `unknown`, NEVER `clean`. A scan that reports only what it found reports a detector that read the code and matched nothing, a detector the ScanProfile switched off, and a detector that cannot express the way this project spells the thing, as one and the same nothing - and the reader cannot tell any of them from a repository that is genuinely in order. Measured in this repository's own G3 mutation harness: 212 of the 450 mutants that record it take their whole file to zero candidates, so the rule goes silent and nothing anywhere says so. This array is what the adjudicating agent reasons over; findings.candidates is the other half and the two never overlap - a rule that raised a candidate is not repeated here, because a fact two places must agree on is kept in one. Rules the installed packs do not ship are in neither: this array is built from the loaded bundle, so it never reports on a rule that was not there. NOTHING HERE IS A FINDING ABOUT THE CODE, and no consumer may read a row as a defect in the scanned repository. JURISDICTION IS CARRIED AND NEVER APPLIED - see the `jurisdiction` property. ONE SILENCE THIS ARRAY DOES NOT DISTINGUISH, stated rather than left to be found: a rule whose every match was removed by a `detector.guard_missing` guard appears here as `evaluated` with no marker, because a suppressed match never becomes a candidate. Those removals are listed in `suppressed_by_guard`, which a reader must consult alongside this array; 0 of the bundle's 56 rules declare `guard_missing` today, which is the only reason the case is inert rather than merely rare. The corroboration gate, which 9 rules do declare, is marked per row in `matches_removed_by_corroboration`.

rule_id.description: The rule that produced nothing, on the same terms and with the same pattern as candidates[].rule_id. Shape only: that the id names a rule the bundle ships is a fact about two documents, which no schema can state - it is asserted by the workspace's findings-schema check against the built bundle, as suppressed_by_corroboration[].rule_id is.

title.description: Title of the rule, copied verbatim, so the record reads on its own. The length limit is rule.schema.json's own, for the same reason as candidates[].title's. IT IS A HAND-KEPT COPY AND, UNLIKE candidates[].title, NO SEAM COMPARISON COVERS IT: compareSeam() in the workspace's findings-schema check has four call sites - rule to candidates[], checklist to applicability[] and to applicability[].limbs[], and the bundle manifest to bundle.version - and none of them covers rules_without_candidates[], so a drift between this number and rule.schema.json's would pass every gate. Independent verification confirmed that on 2026-09-04 by reading all four of those call sites. An earlier revision of this sentence credited that verification with a measurement of a field called `silent_rules`, which is not a property of this schema at all; the measurement was vacuous and the name was wrong, and both are corrected here rather than quietly dropped. Raised from 120 to 160 with rule.schema.json's on 2026-09-03, and from 160 to 180 on 2026-09-04.

state.description: `evaluated`: the rule was in scope and raised no candidate, AND THAT IS ALL THIS VALUE SAYS. It does not by itself mean the detector read anything: `files_on_surface` of 0 means the rule was offered no file at all, and a non-zero `matches_removed_by_corroboration` means its own patterns DID match and a corroboration gate then silenced them. Only a row with `files_on_surface` above zero and no corroboration removals is the one where the detector read code and matched none of it; THAT is the `unknown` POPULATION and the one an adjudicator must reason about, and even there a detector that did not find something has not established that the construct is absent. This description said "the rule ran over this tree and matched nothing ... `not-evaluated`: the ScanProfile's own answers put the rule out of scope before it read a line, and `unmet_preconditions` names which answers; nothing was looked at, so this is evidence about the declaration and not about the code. The two are separate values rather than one flag because collapsing them is exactly the conflation this array exists to remove. FROM 2026-08-27 THIS SCANNER NEVER WRITES not-evaluated: a profile answer labels a rule's output and no longer removes the rule, so every row is evaluated and the rows that used to be not-evaluated are the ones now carrying declared_inapplicable_preconditions. The value stays in the enum because documents written before that date carry it and every consumer has to keep reading them.

jurisdiction.description: The rule's own declared jurisdictions, copied verbatim from rule.schema.json's `jurisdiction`. CARRIED, NEVER APPLIED: nothing in the CLI compares this with ScanProfile.distribution_regions, and no row is dropped, hidden or marked out-of-scope on the strength of it. That comparison belongs to the adjudicating agent, which already makes it for candidates (product/plugin/skills/legal-scan/SKILL.md, 'if a rule's jurisdiction is absent from the profile's distribution_regions, return not_applicable'), and it stays in ONE place: a per-rule jurisdiction gate was written into the engine on 2026-07-27 and removed the same day on the owner's correction, because the region choice belongs to pack selection and repeating it inside the scan deletes candidates silently (product/packages/cli/src/engine.ts, preconditionsMet). It is also not a string comparison - a rule declaring ["EU"] is in scope for a profile declaring ["DE","FR"] - so a mechanical test here would be wrong as well as duplicated.

evidence_template.description: The rule author's account of what a match establishes and what it does not, copied verbatim from the rule's `evidence_template` exactly as candidates[].evidence_template is. THIS IS THE FIELD THAT MAKES THE RECORD USABLE rather than a list of names: read backwards it is the best available statement of what the rule was looking for, which is what an adjudicator needs in order to decide whether this silence is surprising in THIS project against THIS declared profile. The same field was authored in all 56 rules, validated by the build, shipped inside the bundle - and copied into no output at all until 2026-08-11, so it reached neither the adjudicating agent nor the user. A roster that named rules and dropped it would repeat that defect one array over. It is required here for that reason, and all 56 rules of the bundle of 2026-08-19 declare one (52 to 3,665 characters). '{file}' and '{line}' are left unsubstituted as they are on a candidate; here they have no location to stand for at all, which is precisely the state being reported. THE RULE'S `context_questions` AND `legal_basis` ARE DELIBERATELY NOT HERE: they ship whole inside the bundle the reader of this array already has open, and copying them into every scan measured 651 KB of an 879 KB document on the demo tree - 274 KB of questions and 377 KB of quoted provisions for 45 rules that raised nothing - which layer 2 would read at the user's expense. A consumer that wants them opens $LEGAL_BUNDLE_DIR/rules.json for the one or two rules it decides to investigate. A candidate carries them because a candidate is posted to a fresh subagent with no bundle beside it; a row here is not.

effective_date.description: Date the obligation behind this rule starts to apply, copied verbatim from the rule, on the same terms as candidates[].effective_date. Present only where the rule declares one; an absent field means 'the rule states no date', never 'the duty applies now'.

unmet_preconditions.description: The `applicability_preconditions` expressions that did not hold, verbatim from the rule. Present only when `state` is `not-evaluated`, and never empty there, because they are the whole reason the rule did not run. Named rather than counted: stats.rules_suppressed_by_precondition has carried the count since the first scan and has never been able to say which rule or which answer, so a reader who wanted to check a declaration had nothing to check it against. The expression names a field of the reader's OWN ScanProfile - which is the one input they can verify against their own README and their own product. NO LONGER WRITTEN BY THIS SCANNER, AND KEPT BECAUSE DOCUMENTS ALREADY ON DISK CARRY IT. From 2026-08-27 a profile answer does not stop a rule from running, so no row this scanner writes is not-evaluated and this field has no row to sit on; declared_inapplicable_preconditions carries the same expressions for the rules that used to be here.

unanswered_preconditions.description: The applicability_preconditions expressions this rule turns on that the profile does not answer at all, verbatim from the rule. Present only when non-empty, and on EITHER state: a rule can be switched off by one answered precondition while a second is left open, and both belong in front of the reader before they decide whether the declaration is right. UNANSWERED IS NOT not_applicable. Until 2026-08-25 an unanswered precondition was read as an answer of no and the rule never ran; it runs now, and the legal-scan skill requires this row to be reported as unknown with the open question named.

declared_inapplicable_preconditions.description: The applicability_preconditions this rule turns on that the profile ANSWERED in a way that puts the rule out of scope, verbatim - and the rule ran anyway. Present only when non-empty. THIS FIELD SAYS THE RULE WAS ALLOWED TO RUN UNDER AN ANSWER OF NO, AND IT SAYS NOTHING ON ITS OWN ABOUT WHAT THE RULE THEN READ OR MATCHED. Which of the three silences this row is, is read from the OTHER fields of this same row and never from this one: files_on_surface above zero with no matches_removed_by_corroboration is the only shape that supports the words 'the detector was allowed to look for it and it found nothing', and only that shape corroborates the declaration - weakly, since a detector that did not find a construct has not established that the construct is absent. files_on_surface of 0 means no file was offered to the rule at all, so this pass neither contradicted nor corroborated the answer. A non-zero matches_removed_by_corroboration means the rule's own patterns DID match here and a corroboration gate then removed them, which is the opposite of a corroboration: the construct is in this tree. This description asserted the corroboration unconditionally until 2026-08-27, when independent verification reproduced a console line built the same way calling a gate-silenced rule and a rule with no surface 'answered out of scope and raised nothing' - on a screen that said four lines above that the construct was in the tree, and on an empty directory with files 0 scanned. These are the same expressions unmet_preconditions used to carry, under a different name because the fact is different: that one says the rule never ran, and SKILL.md step 3b tells an agent to report it as not_applicable.

files_on_surface.description: How many of the files this scan opened the rule was allowed to read: the files that passed its `detector.file_globs` (or the non-production default) and were not carved out by its `detector.path_without`. Present only when `state` is `evaluated`. ZERO IS THE READING THIS FIELD EXISTS FOR. A rule offered no file has said nothing about the code - its silence is a fact about the tree's layout and the rule's declared surface. A rule that read four thousand files and matched none of them has said something quite different. Both produce zero candidates, and no output could tell them apart before 2026-08-19. It counts files OFFERED and never files that matched: no `match` clause is consulted, so it moves with the walk and the surface declarations and with nothing a detector decides. It is a count and never a filter - nothing reads it back, so it cannot change which candidate is raised.

context_payloads.description: THE INDEX OF THE PER-GROUP PAYLOAD FILES THIS RUN WROTE BESIDE THIS DOCUMENT, AND THOSE FILES HOLD VERBATIM SOURCE CODE FROM THE SCANNED TREE. Added 2026-09-17. One file per adjudication_group.key, each carrying that group's candidates together with the neighbourhood of every matched line: up to window_lines lines each side, the file's first contiguous import region, and the opening line of each enclosing construct the structural reading recorded - all of it copied verbatim, with the file's own line numbers, by layer 1 and with no model call. SINCE 2026-09-18 A PAYLOAD WRITES THE RULE'S OWN PROSE ONCE AND NOT ONCE PER CANDIDATE (layer-2 cost lane, unit P(a)): the eight fields that belong to the rule rather than to the candidate - title, evidence_template, remediation_template, context_questions, legal_basis_refs, data_categories, effective_date, depends_on_applicability - are in the payload's own rules array, one block per rule id, and each candidate names its block with the rule_id it already carries. NOTHING WAS DROPPED, SHORTENED OR SUMMARISED AND THIS DOCUMENT DID NOT CHANGE: the same values, in the same file, written once, and the only thing that moves here is each index row's bytes and sha256. Repeating the prose under every candidate had taken the largest payload of the three measured trees to 1,325,971 B, about 331k tokens, which is more than a child can be handed at all; it is 305,031 B now, and every payload of all three trees is under 400,000 B. See an internal record. WHY BESIDE THE DOCUMENT AND NOT IN IT: measured at 40 lines each side, putting the windows in this document takes the largest tree read from 19.7 MB to about 70.9 MB per location, or about 33.8 MB deduplicated per file, and the consumer of this document is an agent opening it with a Read tool; one file per group leaves the document at 19.7 MB and gives the orchestrator one small file to read per child. The measured median excerpt text per payload is in the producing module's own header (product/packages/cli/src/context.ts) and is deliberately not repeated here: a measured number kept in two places goes stale in one of them, and this description's copy did (it said 4.7 kB on the largest tree, taken before the per-location floor was raised). DATA LOCALITY: the payload files are written under the directory --out names - the user's own .legal/ on a default run - and nothing about them leaves the machine, but a person who shares a payload file SHARES CODE, which is a stronger act than sharing this document, and it is said here rather than left to be discovered. PRESENT ONLY WHERE --out NAMED A DOCUMENT TO WRITE THEM BESIDE AND THE EXCERPTS ARE ON: --context-window 0 or PRODUCT_CLI_CONTEXT=0 turns them off and this key is then absent, and the document is then byte-for-byte the document written before this key existed. window_lines.description: Lines each side of a matched line the excerpts were built with (--context-window, 40 by default). It is a CEILING and not a promise: the window is also bounded by max_bytes_per_location and max_bytes_per_payload below, and by the file's own first and last line, and an excerpt stopped short of it says so in its own short_of_window field. 0 is not a value here - the excerpts are off at 0 and this whole key is absent.

max_bytes_per_location.description: The most excerpt text one location may be given. A HARD CEILING, and the only one here: measured on the three prepared trees at 40 lines each side, the per-location window is a median of 2.5 kB on the largest of them, 4.9 kB at p90 and 11.9 kB at its maximum, so it bites at the top of the distribution and on files whose lines are long. THE MATCHED LINES THEMSELVES ARE NEVER SHORTENED BY IT: they are the one text a verdict must quote.

min_bytes_per_location.description: The least excerpt text one location is given however many locations share its payload - about 40 lines of ordinary source. bytes_per_payload_budget below YIELDS TO THIS, and that direction is the point: the figure this whole mechanism rests on is that 40 of the 75 not_applicable verdicts of one measured real run rest entirely on evidence within 30 lines of the matched line, so a budget that cannot hold that much is a window not worth writing. Measured on one large tree's 14,143 locations: at a floor of 600 bytes the median location was given a 57-line window and 3,242 were given under 41 lines; at this figure the median is 77 and 1,522 are under 41, and those are in files whose lines are long, where max_bytes_per_location and not this is what binds.

bytes_per_payload_budget.description: The excerpt budget one payload file is given, divided evenly over its locations and then clamped between min_bytes_per_location and max_bytes_per_location. A BUDGET AND NOT A CEILING: a payload holding many locations ends up above this figure rather than below the floor, and a payload holds excerpts for at most MAX_LOCATIONS_PER_ADJUDICATION (70) READING UNITS - every location where the candidates are read line by line, and the representative of each same-kind line group plus the first line of each of its largest sub-shapes where a candidate carries a `kinds` census, never every member - so the worst case is 70 times max_bytes_per_location as it was and the ordinary large case is 70 times the floor. What it buys, measured on the largest tree read: it binds on payloads holding between about 16 and 44 locations and takes the largest payload's excerpt text from about 195 kB to 161 kB, leaving the median (5 kB) untouched.

max_bytes_per_payload.description: The most bytes a payload file holding MORE THAN ONE candidate may have (400,000). Unlike the three figures above, which shape the excerpt text, this one divides the BIN: a bin whose assembled payload is over it is cut by reading units, in the bin's order, until every part is under it or holds one candidate, and each part is renumbered and rekeyed in the packer's own bin:<n>#<rules> form. It exists because the unit bound cannot see bytes - a bin of 70 reading units opening 174 locations reaches about 570 kB while breaking no bound it was given - and because SKILL.md step 4 hands a payload to a child by PASTING IT INLINE, so at about 4 bytes per token this figure is about 100k tokens of that child's window spent before it reads anything of its own. Measured on one large tree before the cap: 58 payloads, median 234,185 B, maximum 572,215 B, eleven at or over this figure. Written only where the scan packed its payloads: --pack-groups off writes the index this scanner wrote before the cap existed, field for field.
max_bytes_per_payload.$comment: Added by unit S1-a of the layer-2 unit-of-judgment design.

payloads_oversized.description: How many payload files this run wrote over max_bytes_per_payload. Every one of them holds a single candidate, whose own adjudication_group carries payload_bytes and oversized where the payload is that candidate's seat. A cost, stated: it is the number of children that will be handed more than the cap, and it cannot be lowered by dividing anything. Written only where the scan packed its payloads.
payloads_oversized.$comment: Added by unit S1-a of the layer-2 unit-of-judgment design.

bins_divided_by_cap.description: How many of the packer's bins the byte cap divided. A bin cut into three parts counts once. The parts are in payloads[] under their own keys, so this number is the difference between the bins the packer made and the payload files this run wrote, and nothing else in this document has to be read to learn it. Written only where the scan packed its payloads.
bins_divided_by_cap.$comment: Added by unit S1-a of the layer-2 unit-of-judgment design.

holds_source_excerpts.description: Always true, and written rather than implied. It is the one field a consumer can test to learn that this run produced files holding source code, without having to know what a payload file is.

launches.description: Adjudicator launches this document implies: ONE PER PAYLOAD FILE, reader payloads included. The one EXACT number in this object - everything else here is derived from it and from a measured constant.

candidates.description: Distinct candidates those launches adjudicate, by finding_id. A candidate read by kinds occupies several payload files and is still one candidate.

read_tokens_per_payload_byte.description: Tokens one payload byte costs a seat that reads it (the readers of two runs on two open-source repositories, averaged).

verdict_tokens_per_one_seat_candidate.description: Tokens a verdict costs a one-seat bin beyond its reading (two runs averaged, make-ups included).

answer_seat_tokens.description: Tokens one answer seat costs, for a candidate read by readers (two runs averaged, make-ups included).

orchestration_tokens_per_launch.description: Tokens of the relays and the main session per launch (two runs averaged, after the run-shape answer).

second_check_tokens_per_violation_candid.description: Tokens one refuter costs (live run 2, scaled to count each hand-back output as run fm1 does).

violation_candidate_share.description: Violation candidates per candidate adjudicated, low and high (run 2; the larger of the two runs): how many refuters the second check launches is known only after the verdicts.

host_over_priced.description: The host record over the seats priced tokens, low and high (the smoke 1.015; the larger of the two runs, 1.27 and 1.29; the gap is not explained).

widened.description: Multipliers of the central figure for the low and high ends: the coefficients are tuning numbers from two repositories.

source.description: Where the model was measured, cited so a reader can re-take it rather than trust it.

price_model.description: THE PRICE MODEL: the lines of two runs on two open-source repositories, so the figures are ranges. Producer: cost-preview.ts PRICE_MODEL.

seconds_per_launch.description: Wall seconds one launch takes WHATEVER IT IS HANDED (a child holding one location and a child holding fifty perform the same investigation ritual).

concurrency.description: Children the skill keeps in flight (design E, ideas.md section E; SKILL.md step 4).

shape.description: full adjudicates every payload, then the second check; important adjudicates the payloads that hold a high-severity candidate OR carry a rule this run launches exactly once, leaves the rest for a later run, then the second check; refute_later adjudicates every payload with no second check and is the recommended shape.

launches.description: Launches this shape spends IN THIS RUN. For refute_later this equals full's: its saving is deferred, not avoided.

candidates.description: Distinct candidates this shape adjudicates in this run, counted by finding_id.

estimated_seconds.description: ceil(launches / concurrency) x seconds_per_launch - WHOLE WAVES, the arithmetic SKILL.md step 4 states. Dividing instead of taking whole waves understates a small run, which is where a user looks first.

selected_for_high_severity.description: important only: payloads kept because they hold a candidate of severity high. It OVERLAPS with selected_as_single_launch_rule - a payload kept for both reasons is in both counts - so the two may sum to more than launches. Both are written because a reader deciding whether the shape is honest needs each limb's weight.

selected_as_single_launch_rule.description: important only: payloads kept because a rule of theirs has exactly one payload in this run. This limb is what stops the shape being high-severity-only: a rule whose whole output is one payload costs one launch to cover completely, and dropping it saves one launch and loses a rule.

estimated_tokens_low.description: This shape, the second check included where it runs: the low end of the range.

estimated_tokens_high.description: The high end of the same range.

second_check.description: Whether the shape runs the second check, one refuter per violation candidate, after its verdicts.

second_check_tokens_low.description: Where second_check: the second check own part of the range, low end.

second_check_tokens_high.description: Where second_check: the second check own part of the range, high end.

items.description: One run shape and what it costs. The user chooses one of these before the first adjudicator is launched, and the choice is recorded in the evidence log's run_shape.

shapes.description: ALWAYS ALL THREE AND ALWAYS IN THIS ORDER: full, important, refute_later. A preview that printed only the shape the producer preferred would be the thing this whole mechanism exists to prevent.

estimated_tokens_low.description: Every payload read and judged once with no second check: the low end of the range, tokens counted at the input price.

estimated_tokens_high.description: The high end of the same range. There is no central figure: rates from two repositories are never shown as a point.

cost_preview.description: WHAT LAYER 2 WILL COST OVER THESE PAYLOADS, AND THE THREE SHAPES THE RUN MAY TAKE. Layer 2 runs in the user's own agent and THE USER PAYS FOR IT; until this key existed the first number a user saw was the bill. It sits inside the payload index rather than at the top level because every figure in it is derived from payloads[] below - the launch count IS the row count - and a document with no payload index has no launch count to state. A PURE FUNCTION OF THE DOCUMENT: the producer (product/packages/cli/src/cost-preview.ts) reads no file, no clock and no environment, so two runs of one tree write the same preview. NOTHING HERE IS A DECISION: the scan does not choose a shape and says so on its own last line; the skill asks the person before the first adjudicator is launched and records the answer in the evidence log's run_shape.

payloads.description: One row per adjudication group, in the order this document's candidates first name the group. Every adjudication_group.key in candidates[] has exactly one row and every row names a key the document carries; the orchestrator reads the row's path for the group it is launching a child for, and never opens this whole document per child.

key.description: The adjudication_group.key this file carries, verbatim. READ AS AN OPAQUE STRING AND NEVER AS A PATH: it is the file of the candidate's first location today, with #batch-<n> where one file's candidates were divided, and the shape is the grouping's to choose, not this index's. path below is the only thing that names a file.

path.description: Where the payload file is, relative to the directory this document is in, beginning with directory above. The name is a slug of key with a hash of key appended, so it is deterministic, readable and collision-free whatever shape the key has; a consumer resolves this field and never re-derives the name.

candidates.description: How many candidates the payload carries. Equal to the number of this document's candidates whose adjudication_group.key is key.

locations.description: How many locations the payload OPENS - every one of which is in the payload with a context block naming the excerpt that covers it. For a payload of candidates read line by line that is every location those candidates carry, which is what this field has always said. For a payload holding a candidate read by same-kind line groups it is the representative of each kind the seat was handed plus the first line of each of its largest sub-shapes, and locations_covered beside it says how many matched lines those stand for. ZERO ON ONE SHAPE, AND IT IS NOT AN EMPTY PAYLOAD: the verdict seat's own payload of a candidate whose reading plan gave it readers and no seat slice. The design's verdict seat with readers holds "the bounded summary of the census, the readers' dispositions folded by the CLI" and opens no excerpt of its own; the units are in the `#reader-<n>` rows beside this one, locations_covered says how many matched lines they stand for, and the payload still carries the whole census catalogue.

reading_units.description: How many READING UNITS this payload hands its seat - the same-kind line groups of a candidate carrying a `kinds` census, and the locations of one that does not. WRITTEN ONLY ON A PAYLOAD HOLDING A CANDIDATE READ BY KINDS, so the index of a `--kind-census off` document is byte-for-byte the one written before the census existed. Never above MAX_LOCATIONS_PER_ADJUDICATION (70). ZERO ON THE SAME ONE SHAPE `locations` is zero on, and for the same reason: a verdict seat whose plan gave it readers and no seat slice reads the readers' fold and opens no unit itself (design.md section 3.2). It is the honest count and not a missing value - the candidate's own total is `reading_units` on the candidate in the payload, and the units themselves are handed to the `#reader-<n>` payloads.
reading_units.$comment: Added by unit U2 of the layer-2 unit-of-judgment design.

locations_covered.description: How many of the document's matched locations the candidates in this payload carry ALTOGETHER, which for a candidate read by kinds is far more than the payload opens: one candidate can hold hundreds of kinds over tens of thousands of locations. The difference between this and `locations` is the reading the verdict's own `reading` block accounts for afterwards, member by member. WRITTEN ONLY ON A PAYLOAD HOLDING A CANDIDATE READ BY KINDS.
locations_covered.$comment: Added by unit U2 of the layer-2 unit-of-judgment design.

excerpts.description: How many verbatim source excerpts the payload carries. Fewer than locations wherever two matched lines in one file are near enough for their windows to have been merged into one excerpt, which is the ordinary case and is why the excerpt total is about a third of what one window per location would cost.

bytes.description: The payload file's size in bytes, as written.

sha256.description: The payload file's SHA-256, so a consumer can tell a payload written by this scan from one edited or left over from another. It is a hash of the file as written, including its own copy of scan_id, so it differs between two runs of the same tree exactly as scan_id does.

oversized.description: True where `bytes` is over max_bytes_per_payload, and absent otherwise. The payload then holds ONE candidate: a payload of several is divided by the cap until every part is under it or holds one candidate, and a candidate whose payload alone is over it is written WHOLE - never divided and never shortened, because a candidate is one seat (design annex section 3.2) and a seat handed part of its evidence returns a verdict about part of its evidence. So this flag is what the run says INSTEAD of truncating: the orchestrator handing this payload to a child is being told, before it pastes it, that this one is about 100k tokens of that child's window. Written only where the scan packed its payloads.
oversized.$comment: Added by unit S1-a of the layer-2 unit-of-judgment design.

per_rule_applicability.description: THE QUESTIONS ANSWERED ONCE PER RULE, NOT ONCE PER CANDIDATE. A layer-2 child costs about the same whatever it is handed, so the run's bill is the number of children - and two of the questions every child answers before it reads a line are questions about the RULE rather than about its candidate: whether the rule's jurisdiction reaches the regions the person declared, and what the person answered to the premises the rule declares. Both are facts about the PRODUCT, read from the person's own declaration and never inferred from source vocabulary. THIS BLOCK REMOVES NOTHING: `candidates` and `rules_without_candidates` are byte-for-byte what they were before it existed, and the per-rule region gate the owner took out of the scan on 2026-07-27 is not reopened - that gate deleted candidates silently, and this writes an answer beside them. What acts on the answer is the orchestrator, in legal-scan/SKILL.md step 4, which launches no seat for a rule answered `does_not_apply` and reports its candidates as not applicable by declaration, one record per finding_id. The producer and the whole of the design are product/packages/cli/src/per-rule-applicability.ts.

answered_from.description: The profile field every jurisdiction answer in this block was read from. Always `ScanProfile.distribution_regions`; written rather than assumed so a reader of the document alone can see which declaration the answers rest on.

declared_regions.description: What the person declared, verbatim, or null where they declared nothing this test can use. Quoted here so the answer can be overturned in one line.

regions_not_offered.description: The regions the person answered No to, verbatim, where the profile read carries the list; absent where it does not (a profile written under the earlier closed list, or none). A rule is settled as not applying only when every jurisdiction it declares lies within one of them.

settled.description: Whether the jurisdiction question was settled at all on this run. FALSE means no profile, no distribution_regions, an empty array, or the recorded answer "unknown" - and then every rule is adjudicated and this block removes nothing.

rules.description: One row per rule that raised a candidate, plus every rule that raised none and whose jurisdiction does not apply - the second group is what an evidence log needs to record `out_of_jurisdiction` in unknown_rules without the orchestrator re-deriving it. A rule that raised nothing and applies gets no row: its roster entry already says everything and a row would be bytes the user pays to read.

jurisdiction.description: The rule's own declared jurisdictions, copied. Carried so the reader sees both sides of the judgement.

jurisdiction_question.description: Does this rule's jurisdiction reach the declared regions? THE ONLY QUESTION IN THIS BLOCK THAT CAN REMOVE A LAUNCH.

premise_questions.description: One entry per applicability_preconditions expression the rule declares. NEVER REMOVES A LAUNCH, in either direction: an answer that puts the rule's subject out of scope is a disagreement with the detector that matched the construct anyway, and the standing decision of 2026-08-27 is that such a candidate is reported and never dismissed on the strength of the answer. Settled here so a seat can cite it by name instead of re-deriving it.

adjudicate.description: Whether this rule's candidates are to be adjudicated. False ONLY where jurisdiction_question.answer is `does_not_apply`, or where a `scope` answer from the program's confirmed record puts the rule out of scope (`settled_by`; nv-wp4-questions-2026-11-02.md); no other premise answer moves it.

not_adjudicated_as.description: Present only where `adjudicate` is false. The words the report and the evidence log must use for every candidate of this rule. NEVER SILENTLY DROPPED.

settled_by.description: Present only where a scope answer from a confirmed record settled this rule (`adjudicate` false, no seat runs): the profile field, the answer as given and the date the record holds. The report lists the rule with this scan's place count and the command to change the answer, every scan; a candidate settled this way is never silently dropped.

answer.description: The answer as the confirmed record holds it.

settled_premise.description: THE ONE SENTENCE THE ORCHESTRATOR HANDS TO THE SEAT, once per rule in the bin, in place of the seat deriving the answer itself. It names the rule, the answer, the field the answer came from and the value that field holds, so a seat citing it is citing a declaration and a reader can check it against .legal/profile.json in one line.

groups.description: The adjudication_group keys this rule's candidates sit in, sorted.

launches_removed.description: Launches removed by THIS rule's answer: the launches of the groups that vanish and in which this rule takes part. These do not sum to summary.launches_removed - a bin holding two rules that both answer `does_not_apply` vanishes once and is counted once under each of them.

summary.description: What the answers cost or saved on this run, counted over the groups the scan actually wrote.

rules_not_applicable.description: Rules WITH candidates whose jurisdiction does not reach the declaration.

silent_rules_not_applicable.description: Rules with NO candidate whose jurisdiction does not reach the declaration - the unknown_rules rows that take outcome `out_of_jurisdiction`.

candidates_not_adjudicated.description: Candidates reported as not applicable by declaration. Reported, never removed from `candidates`.

groups_removed.description: Groups EVERY ONE of whose candidates belongs to a rule that does not apply. A bin spans up to three rules by construction, so a bin holding one applying rule still launches.

groups_reduced.description: Groups that still launch although they hold at least one candidate of a rule that does not apply. The saving on them is a shorter payload, not a child.

launches_removed.description: Children not launched: one verdict seat per removed group, plus the reader children those groups carried. REFUTATIONS ARE NOT COUNTED - a refutation depends on a verdict that was never taken - so this is a floor and the run saves at least it.

ships_premises.description: DOES IT SHIP, AS THE PROGRAM READS IT: for every file holding a location, whether the repository's own build and tooling files put it in what ships, decided once at scan time and handed to the seats as a premise they may contradict with a quotation. Never used to skip a file: candidates and locations are the same with and without it. Unknown ships: a premise other than `product` and `unknown` needs a positive signal of a non-shipping class and no signal that a declared artifact includes the file; path names alone are never a signal. Keyed by the file's path as `locations[].file` names it. Absent where the scan computed none: every file is then `unknown`.

because.description: The manifest or toolchain lines the premise rests on, each quoted.

conflict.description: Signals of a non-shipping class that a declared artifact's inclusion overruled (`product` wins), recorded rather than dropped.

perRuleQuestion.description: One settled question: what was asked, what the answer is, where the answer was read, and one sentence quoting both sides so a reader can overturn it in one line.

question.description: The question in words, as the person would be asked it. A fact about the product is ASKED of the person or read from their declared documents, never inferred from the codebase.

answer.description: `applies` / `does_not_apply` / `unanswered` are the jurisdiction question's answers, and `does_not_apply` IS THE ONLY ONE IN THIS BLOCK THAT REMOVES A LAUNCH. `met` / `declared_out_of_scope` / `unanswered` are a premise question's, and none of them removes a launch.

answered_from.description: The profile field the answer was read from, in `ScanProfile.<path>` form. Never a path into the scanned tree: this block answers no question from source.

declared.description: The value read, verbatim, or null where the field was not answered.

because.description: One sentence naming the rule's declaration and the person's, so the answer can be checked and overturned without re-running anything.
